title: Ejercito v. Sandiganbayan
summary: The Supreme Court addressed procedural aspects of plunder cases before the Sandiganbayan, clarifying rules on bail, the right to speedy disposition of cases, and the scope of the Plunder Law in relation to the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.
doctrine: Plunder is a heinous crime and is not bailable when the evidence of guilt is strong. The right to speedy disposition of cases may be invoked when there is unreasonable delay in the proceedings. The Plunder Law is independent of the Anti-Graft Law and both may be applied simultaneously.
fullText:
TINGA, J.:

This case involves various procedural issues in the prosecution of the plunder case before the Sandiganbayan.

Plunder, as defined in Republic Act No. 7080, is committed by any public officer who, by himself or in connivance with members of his family, relatives by affinity or consanguinity, business associates, subordinates, or other persons, amasses, accumulates or acquires ill-gotten wealth through a combination or series of overt criminal acts.

The right to bail is not absolute. Under the Constitution, bail is a matter of right only before conviction, except in cases where the offense charged is punishable by reclusion perpetua or death and the evidence of guilt is strong. Plunder, being a capital offense, requires a hearing to determine the strength of the evidence.
